Well-differentiated small hepatocellular carcinoma is not typically considered to be a "clinically early" cancer. In fact, studies have shown that patients with well-differentiated HCC (Hepatocellular Carcinoma) often do not experience significant differences in disease-free survival compared to those with poorly differentiated or intermediate-grade HCC.

Well-differentiated small HCC typically refers to tumors that are composed of hepatocytes and other normal liver cells, and have a low level of cellular atypia. Despite its slow growth rate, well-differentiated small HCC can still be aggressive and may require prompt treatment.

In general, patients with well-differentiated small HCC often face a similar prognosis as those with poorly differentiated or intermediate-grade HCC, which is typically poor due to the tumor's small size, low grade, and limited cellular atypia. 

It's essential to note that these findings are based on data from local datasets and may not be representative of all patients. Further research is needed to better understand the prognostic implications of well-differentiated small HCC and its treatment outcomes.
